positions/molinism/oneLine: God’s "middle knowledge" of what every free creature would do in any circumstance lets him providentially ordain all things and give efficacious grace without overriding libertarian freedom.
positions/molinism/coreClaims/0: God has natural knowledge (what could be), middle knowledge (what free creatures would do in any situation) and free knowledge (what will be).
positions/molinism/coreClaims/1: By choosing which world and which circumstances to actualise, God sovereignly arranges salvation history.
positions/molinism/coreClaims/2: Grace is efficacious not intrinsically but through the free consent God foresaw.
positions/molinism/coreClaims/3: Human beings retain libertarian freedom to accept or refuse grace.
positions/molinism/origin: Luis de Molina, Concordia liberi arbitrii cum gratiae donis (Lisbon 1588); fought out with the Dominicans in the Congregatio de Auxiliis (1597-1607), which Pope Paul V closed without condemning either side.
positions/molinism/strongestArguments/0: It reconciles strong providence with genuine freedom, avoiding both fatalism and open theism.
positions/molinism/strongestArguments/1: Scripture appears to show God knowing counterfactuals (David at Keilah; Tyre and Sidon).
positions/molinism/strongestArguments/2: It has been revived in analytic philosophy of religion as a solution to the problem of evil.
positions/molinism/strongestObjections/0: The "grounding objection": what makes counterfactuals of freedom true before any creature exists?
positions/molinism/strongestObjections/1: Dominicans: it makes God dependent on creatures and grace dependent on human consent.
positions/molinism/strongestObjections/2: Calvinists: it still leaves God choosing which free responses to actualise, so it does not remove the problem it seeks to solve.
positions/molinism/responses/0: Molinists answer that counterfactuals need no grounding beyond themselves, as with other necessary truths.
positions/molinism/responses/1: They add that God’s choice of worlds is wise and loving, and that freedom is real within it.
positions/molinism/consequences/0: Permitted alongside Thomism in Catholic theology since 1607.
positions/molinism/consequences/1: Popular among evangelical philosophers since the 1970s.
positions/jansenism/oneLine: A rigorous Catholic Augustinianism teaching that fallen humanity is wholly dependent on irresistible efficacious grace, joined to strict moral and sacramental discipline.
positions/jansenism/coreClaims/0: After the fall the will is enslaved to concupiscence without efficacious grace.
positions/jansenism/coreClaims/1: Efficacious grace infallibly moves the will by a "victorious delight"; "sufficient grace" that does not suffice is an illusion.
positions/jansenism/coreClaims/2: Christ did not die for all in the same way; the number of elect is small.
positions/jansenism/coreClaims/3: Moral rigour: perfect contrition, infrequent communion, opposition to Jesuit casuistry.
positions/jansenism/origin: Cornelius Jansen’s posthumous Augustinus (1640), championed by Saint-Cyran, Antoine Arnauld, Pascal and the convent of Port-Royal; five propositions condemned by Innocent X (Cum occasione, 1653), the movement by Clement XI (Unigenitus, 1713).
positions/jansenism/strongestArguments/0: It claims to be faithful to Augustine, the doctor of grace, against Jesuit innovations.
positions/jansenism/strongestArguments/1: It produced remarkable piety and literature (Pascal’s Pensées and Provincial Letters).
positions/jansenism/strongestArguments/2: It opposed moral laxity in confession.
positions/jansenism/strongestObjections/: Rome: the five propositions (including that Christ did not die for all) are heretical.
Jesuits: it is crypto-Calvinism that denies sufficient grace and God’s universal saving will.
Critics note its rigour discouraged sacramental life.
positions/jansenism/responses/0: Jansenists distinguished "right" from "fact": the propositions were heretical but not in Jansen’s book.
positions/jansenism/responses/1: Defenders point out that it remained Catholic in sacramental and ecclesial practice.
positions/jansenism/consequences/0: Divided the French church for a century; Port-Royal was razed (1710-12).
positions/jansenism/consequences/1: Contributed to the Old Catholic Church of Utrecht (1723) and to Gallican and anti-Jesuit politics.
positions/justification-by-faith-alone/o: Sinners are declared righteous before God freely, for Christ’s sake alone, through faith alone; Christ’s righteousness is reckoned to them, and good works follow as fruit, not as cause.
positions/justification-by-faith-alone/c: Justification is a forensic (declarative) act: God forgives sins and accounts the believer righteous for Christ’s sake.
Faith alone — trust in God’s promise — receives Christ and his righteousness; works contribute nothing to justification.
The believer is simul iustus et peccator, at once righteous and a sinner.
Through faith the soul is united with Christ in a "joyful exchange", and freely serves the neighbour in love.
positions/justification-by-faith-alone/o: Luther’s "Reformation breakthrough" on Romans 1:17 (dated variously 1513-1519), set out in The Freedom of a Christian (1520), the Augsburg Confession Art. IV (1530) and Melanchthon’s Apology (1531); clarified by the Formula of Concord (1577).
positions/justification-by-faith-alone/s: Paul explicitly says a person is justified "by faith apart from works of the law" (Rom 3:28) and that God "justifies the ungodly" (Rom 4:5).
It gives troubled consciences assurance by resting salvation on Christ’s work, not on one’s own progress.
It magnifies grace and Christ’s sufficiency, excluding all boasting.
Catholic: "By works a man is justified, and not by faith only" (Jas 2:24); a merely declared righteousness seems a legal fiction.
It seems to separate justification from sanctification and may encourage antinomianism.
New Perspective: Paul’s "works of the law" concerns Jewish boundary markers, not moral achievement, so the Lutheran reading misframes Paul.
positions/justification-by-faith-alone/r: Lutherans answer that James addresses dead faith, not the ground of justification; living faith always works by love.
God’s declaration is creative, not fictional: the word that forgives also makes new, and faith unites to the living Christ.
positions/justification-by-faith-alone/c: Split Western Christianity; became the "article by which the church stands or falls".
Re-examined in the Lutheran-Catholic Joint Declaration (1999).
positions/tridentine-justification/oneLi: Justification is not only the remission of sins but the sanctification and renewal of the inner person through the voluntary reception of grace; faith is its beginning, charity its form.
positions/tridentine-justification/coreC: Prevenient grace, without any merit, calls the sinner; the person freely assents to and cooperates with that grace.
Justification is the forgiveness of sins and the infusion of sanctifying grace and charity; its instrumental cause is baptism.
Faith is "the beginning, foundation and root" of justification, but faith alone without hope and charity does not unite perfectly with Christ.
Justification can increase through good works, be lost by mortal sin, and be restored through penance; eternal life is both grace and reward.
positions/tridentine-justification/origi: Defined at the Council of Trent, Session VI, 13 January 1547 (16 chapters, 33 canons), after the failed Regensburg compromise on "double justification" (1541).
positions/tridentine-justification/stron: It holds together forgiveness and real transformation, as in Titus 3:5 and Romans 5:5.
It honours the many New Testament texts on judgement according to works and the necessity of love.
It affirms the priority of grace (canons 1-3 condemn Pelagianism) while preserving human cooperation.
Protestants: by making infused righteousness the formal cause of justification it grounds acceptance on a work within us and undermines assurance.
Its anathemas against "faith alone" were often aimed at a caricature of Protestant teaching.
Merit language, however qualified, seems to compromise sola gratia.
positions/tridentine-justification/respo: Catholics answer that merit is itself grace, and that the Protestant view risks separating Christ’s righteousness from the believer’s real holiness.
The 1999 Joint Declaration concluded that Trent’s condemnations do not apply to the Lutheran teaching as presented there.
positions/tridentine-justification/conse: Fixed Catholic identity for the Counter-Reformation.
The benchmark for later ecumenical dialogue (ARCIC, JDDJ).
positions/calvinism-tulip/oneLine: Salvation is wholly God’s sovereign work: by unconditional election, particular redemption and effectual grace, God saves those he chose in Christ and keeps them to the end.
positions/calvinism-tulip/coreClaims/0: Total depravity: sin affects every faculty, so no one can turn to God unaided.
positions/calvinism-tulip/coreClaims/1: Unconditional election: God chooses whom he will save, not on the basis of foreseen faith.
positions/calvinism-tulip/coreClaims/2: Limited (definite) atonement: Christ’s death is sufficient for all but intended to secure the salvation of the elect.
positions/calvinism-tulip/coreClaims/3: Irresistible (effectual) grace: the Spirit infallibly regenerates the elect; and perseverance of the saints: the truly regenerate cannot finally fall away.
positions/calvinism-tulip/coreClaims/4: For Calvin, all benefits come by union with Christ through the Spirit, yielding the "double grace" of justification and sanctification.
positions/calvinism-tulip/origin: Rooted in Augustine and Calvin’s Institutes (1559, III.21-24); codified by the Synod of Dort (1618-19) against the Remonstrants; "TULIP" is an English mnemonic of the early 20th century.
positions/calvinism-tulip/strongestArgum: It is the natural reading of Romans 9 and Ephesians 1 and of Jesus’ words that none can come unless the Father draws them.
It gives all glory to God and grounds assurance in God’s faithfulness rather than human resolve.
It has inspired missions (Carey, Whitefield, Edwards) and the conviction that preaching is God’s means of calling the elect.
positions/calvinism-tulip/strongestObjec: Arminians: it contradicts God’s universal love (John 3:16; 1 Tim 2:4; 2 Pet 3:9) and makes the gospel offer insincere to the non-elect.
Orthodox and Catholics: it makes God the author of reprobation and denies real human cooperation.
Some Reformed (Amyraldians, Barth) object to limited atonement and to a decree behind the back of Jesus Christ.
positions/calvinism-tulip/responses/0: Calvinists answer that God’s universal love and particular saving love are distinct, and that the free offer is sincere because all who come are received.
positions/calvinism-tulip/responses/1: Reprobation is God’s just passing over of sinners, not the cause of their sin (Westminster Confession 3.7).
positions/calvinism-tulip/consequences/0: Defining doctrine of continental Reformed and Presbyterian churches; animated Puritanism and the First Great Awakening.
positions/calvinism-tulip/consequences/1: A "Young, Restless, Reformed" resurgence among evangelicals since the 2000s.
positions/arminianism/oneLine: God sincerely wills all to be saved: by prevenient grace he enables every hearer to believe, elects in Christ those who believe, and saves through grace that can be resisted.
positions/arminianism/coreClaims/0: Fallen humans cannot believe without grace, but prevenient grace restores the ability to respond.
positions/arminianism/coreClaims/1: Election is in Christ and conditional on foreseen faith (or corporate, in Christ as the Elect One).
positions/arminianism/coreClaims/2: Christ died for all people; his atonement is universal in intent though effective only for believers.
positions/arminianism/coreClaims/3: Grace is resistible; whether believers can finally fall away was left open in 1610 and later often affirmed.
positions/arminianism/origin: Jacobus Arminius (1560-1609), Leiden professor, criticised Beza’s supralapsarianism; after his death the Five Articles of the Remonstrance (1610) were rejected at Dort (1618-19). Later forms: Grotius and Limborch (Remonstrant), Wesleyan "evangelical Arminianism".
positions/arminianism/strongestArguments: It takes at face value Scripture’s declarations of God’s universal love and Christ’s death for all.
It preserves the sincerity of the gospel offer and human moral responsibility.
Arminius himself insisted that it is fully a theology of grace: all good is from grace, which is necessary at every step.
positions/arminianism/strongestObjection: Calvinists: conditional election makes the human decision the decisive factor and leaves room for boasting.
If grace is resistible, God’s purposes may fail and Christ might die for no one in particular.
Dort judged it a revival of semi-Pelagianism.
positions/arminianism/responses/0: Arminians reply that receiving a gift by faith is not meritorious, and that God sovereignly chose to save through freely given faith.
positions/arminianism/responses/1: They distinguish their view from semi-Pelagianism by insisting grace precedes and enables the first movement of faith.
positions/arminianism/consequences/0: Remonstrant clergy deposed and banished after Dort; tolerated in the Netherlands from 1630.
positions/arminianism/consequences/1: Through Wesley, the dominant soteriology of Methodist, Holiness and Pentecostal Christianity and much global evangelicalism.
